etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English product, from Latin prōductus, perfect participle of prōdūcō, first attested in English in the mathematics sense.

definitions.definition: The amount of an artifact that has been created by someone or some process.
A consequence of someone's efforts or of a particular set of circumstances.
(chemistry) A chemical substance formed as a result of a chemical reaction.
(arithmetic) A quantity obtained by multiplication of two or more numbers.
(mathematics) Any operation or a result thereof which generalises multiplication of numbers, like the multiplicative operation in a ring, product of types or a categorical product.
Any tangible or intangible good or service that is a result of a process and that is intended for delivery to a customer or end user.

quote.citation: 2002, Oonagh McDonald with Kevin Keasey, The future of retail banking in Europe, page 146:
quote.text: Product innovation is needed to meet changes in society and its requirements for particular types of banking product.

quote.citation: 2002, Veljko Milutinović with Frédéric Patricelli, E-business and e-challenges, page 133:
quote.text: This sort of relationship can improve quality of transportation and can help in negotiations between transportation providers and transportation product users.

quote.citation: 2006, Teresa Luckey with Joseph Phillips, Software project management for dummies, page 55:
quote.text: You can't create a stellar software product unless you know what it is supposed to do. You must work with the stakeholders to create the product scope.

definitions.definition: Anything that is produced; a result.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book XI”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 683-84:
quote.text: To whom thus Michael: These are the product / Of those ill-mated marriages thou sawest;

quote.citation: 1790, Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France:
quote.text: These institutions are the products of enthusiasm; they are the instruments of wisdom.

quote.citation: 2014 June 21, “Magician’s brain”, in The Economist, volume 411, number 8892:
quote.text: The truth is that [Isaac] Newton was very much a product of his time. The colossus of science was not the first king of reason, Keynes wrote after reading Newton’s unpublished manuscripts. Instead “he was the last of the magicians”.

definitions.definition: (US, slang) Illegal drugs, especially cocaine, when viewed as a commodity.
(countable, uncountable) A commodity offered for sale.
(cosmetics, uncountable) Any preparation to be applied to the hair, skin, nails, etc. Often specifically a preparation used to hold one's hair in a desired arrangement.

quote.citation: 2020, Brandon Taylor, Real Life, Daunt Books Originals, page 153:
quote.text: He puts his fingers in Miller’s hair, which is greasy with product.

quote.citation: 1651, The Touchstone of Common Assurances, page 498:
quote.text: The probate of a Testament is the producting and insinuating of it before the Ecclesiastical Judge  […]
